Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander in Iraq, said Sunday he believes U.S. troops will be out of the country by the end of 2011. Gen. Ray Odierno says the U.S. is working with Iraq to maintain security improvements as it looks to withdraw. On CNN's "State of the Union," chief national correspondent John King asked Odierno to rate his confidence, on a scale of 1 to 10, that U.S. troops would be out by the end of the timeline agreed by the U.S. and Iraqi governments. "As you ask me today, I believe it's a 10 -- that we will be gone by 2011," Odierno responded. One of the key architects of the troop "surge" strategy in Iraq, Odierno said conditions in the war-torn country have "improved significantly" in the past year or so. "Obviously, we still have some very serious incidents ... but, again, it's much safer," he said. Nine U.S. troops were killed in March, the lowest monthly toll since the beginning of the Iraq War in 2003, he said.  Watch Odierno share his assessment with CNN's John King » . "So, there's been a clear improvement of security here," Odierno said. "The issue is: Can we maintain that? Can the Iraqis maintain it? And that's what we're working through now. We want them to be able to maintain this stability as we pull out." But less than two weeks into April, the U.S. toll for the month is already at nine. Asked whether the attacks were a sign of increased coordinated violence, Odierno responded that "there are some cells out there who are still capable of conducting suicide attacks," though he described the cells as "very small."  Watch as general discusses joining Facebook » . The U.S. military has made it more difficult for foreign fighters to get into Iraq through Syria, but there is still support for the Iraqi insurgency coming from Iran, he said. Mowaffak al-Rubaie, Iraqi national security adviser, said the Iraqi government is making improvements in handling its own security. "We, the government of Iraq and the security forces in Iraq are much more suited now for this fight," al-Rubaie told "State of the Union." "And we believe that now we are leading and we are planning and carrying out most of the combat operations in the country, " he said, "and the United States forces are moving or transitioning to a more support role, more training, more providing more logistical support, rather than engaging in a huge military or kinetic combat operations." Al-Rubaie was mum when asked how President Obama has differed from former President George W. Bush.  Watch al-Rubaie discuss Iraq's future » . "I don't want to elaborate on differences," al-Rubaie said. "But I believe that President Obama understands the situation in Iraq and I believe he wants to stick by ... the withdrawal agreement." Odierno described Obama as "very attentive." "He listens. He's incredibly intelligent. He talks through the issues," Odierno said. "He makes a decision and then we execute those decisions, and that's all you can expect out of your commander-in-chief. And I've been very pleased with the interaction that I've been able to have with him."

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- On Sunday, General Ray Odierno, America's senior military leader in Iraq, expressed his conviction that American forces would have departed the nation before 2011 draws to a close. According to Odierno, the United States is collaborating with Iraq to preserve the gains made in security as it prepares to pull its forces out.

During an appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," John King, the network's chief national correspondent, requested that Odierno measure his certainty on a numerical scale from 1 to 10 regarding whether American forces would depart by the deadline that both the American and Iraqi administrations had established.

"Based on what I know right now, I'd put it at a 10 -- we'll have left by 2011," Odierno replied.

As one of the principal designers of the troop "surge" approach in Iraq, Odierno noted that circumstances in the battle-scarred nation had "improved significantly" over roughly the previous year.

"We clearly continue to face some extremely grave incidents ... yet, once more, the situation is considerably safer," he stated. He pointed out that only nine American service members died during March, marking the fewest deaths in a single month since the Iraq conflict began back in 2003.

"So the security situation here has undeniably gotten better," Odierno said. "The real question is whether we can preserve it. Whether the Iraqis themselves can preserve it. That's precisely what we're addressing at the moment. Our goal is for them to sustain this stability while we withdraw."

However, with fewer than 14 days having passed in April, the American death count for the month had already reached nine.

When questioned about whether these assaults indicated a rise in organized violence, Odierno answered that "certain cells remain out there that still have the ability to carry out suicide bombings," although he characterized these groups as "very small."

The American military has increased the challenges facing foreign combatants attempting to enter Iraq via Syria, yet backing for the Iraqi insurgency continues to flow from Iran, he explained.

Mowaffak al-Rubaie, who serves as Iraq's national security adviser, stated that his government is advancing in managing its own defense.

"Both the Iraqi government and Iraq's security forces are far better equipped for this struggle now," al-Rubaie told "State of the Union." "We're confident that at present we're taking the lead, doing the planning, and executing the majority of combat missions throughout the country," he continued, "while American troops are shifting or transitioning toward a role focused more on support, training, and logistics, instead of participating in massive military or combat operations."

Al-Rubaie stayed quiet when asked to describe how President Obama's approach had contrasted with that of his predecessor, George W. Bush.

"I'd rather not go into the differences," al-Rubaie remarked. "But I'm confident that President Obama grasps what's happening in Iraq, and I believe he intends to honor ... the withdrawal accord."

Odierno characterized Obama as "very attentive."

"He listens carefully. His intelligence is remarkable. He works through the problems," Odierno observed. "He reaches a decision, and then we carry those decisions out -- which is everything you could ask of your commander-in-chief. I've been thoroughly satisfied with the exchanges I've been able to have with him."

# U.S. Commander Expresses Confidence in Iraq Withdrawal Timeline

General Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander in Iraq, expressed complete confidence that American troops would be withdrawn from the country by the end of 2011. His assessment reflected a growing optimism about the trajectory of the U.S. mission in Iraq, even as challenges remained on the ground.

According to Odierno, security conditions across Iraq had improved significantly over the past year, making the country considerably safer than it had been in previous periods. While he acknowledged that serious incidents continued to occur, he emphasized that the overall situation represented a marked improvement from the height of the conflict.

The statistics offered support for this more hopeful outlook. March 2009 saw only nine U.S. troop deaths—the lowest monthly toll since the Iraq War began in 2003. However, this progress came with important caveats: by mid-April, the death toll had already reached nine within just the first two weeks of the month, underscoring that the security gains remained fragile.

Odierno was careful not to overstate the situation. He noted that small insurgent cells retained the capability to carry out suicide attacks, posing a persistent threat to both American and Iraqi forces. He further observed that support for the insurgency continued to flow from Iran, even as tighter controls had reduced the number of foreign fighters entering the country through Syria.

Looking ahead, Odierno identified the central challenge facing the mission: ensuring that both U.S. and Iraqi forces could maintain the hard-won improvements in security and stability as American troops gradually withdrew. The ultimate success of the withdrawal, he suggested, would depend not merely on meeting a timeline, but on preserving the progress that had been achieved throughout the transition.

# U.S. Commander Expresses Full Confidence in 2011 Iraq Withdrawal

Gen. Ray Odierno, the top U.S. military commander in Iraq, discussed the country's security situation and troop withdrawal timeline in a CNN interview, offering a candid assessment of his confidence in meeting the 2011 deadline agreed upon by both the American and Iraqi governments.

When asked to rate his confidence on a scale of one to ten that U.S. forces would complete their withdrawal by the end of 2011, Odierno left no room for doubt. "I'd say it's a ten," he stated, expressing maximum certainty that American troops would depart on schedule in accordance with the security agreement between Washington and Baghdad.

The general's optimism was grounded in the dramatic improvements in Iraq's security landscape. He pointed to significant progress across the country, most notably highlighting that the past month had seen the lowest monthly death toll since the war began in 2003. This milestone represented a stark contrast to the violence that had gripped Iraq during the peak years of the conflict, when sectarian bloodshed and insurgent attacks claimed thousands of lives.

Despite his confidence, Odierno was careful not to paint an overly rosy picture. He acknowledged that serious challenges remained on the ground. Small insurgent cells continued to operate within the country, capable of carrying out attacks that could still threaten stability and undermine public confidence. These groups, though diminished in strength and reach, persisted as a lingering threat to Iraq's fragile security gains.

The general also raised concerns about external influences, specifically citing ongoing Iranian support for certain elements operating inside Iraq. This foreign interference added a layer of complexity to the security situation, as Tehran's involvement had the potential to fuel instability even as overall violence continued to decline.

Nevertheless, Odierno's overall message was one of measured optimism. The combination of improving security metrics, the growing capability of Iraqi security forces, and the framework provided by the bilateral agreement gave him strong assurance that the United States would successfully meet its withdrawal commitments as planned.

# Top U.S. Commander Confident in Iraq Withdrawal Timeline

The top U.S. military commander in Iraq expressed confidence that American troops will complete their withdrawal from the country by the end of 2011, in accordance with the security agreement between Washington and Baghdad.

Speaking on CNN's "State of the Union," General Ray Odierno addressed questions about the pace of the drawdown and the readiness of Iraqi forces to assume full responsibility for their nation's security.

"I believe we will be gone by the end of 2011," Odierno said, referencing the terms of the U.S.-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement, which calls for the complete removal of American forces by December 31, 2011.

## Progress on the Ground

Odierno pointed to improving conditions across Iraq as evidence that the timeline remains achievable. The general noted that Iraqi security forces have grown increasingly capable of managing security operations, though he acknowledged that challenges remain.

The commander emphasized that the transition would be conditions-based in its execution, but that the overall trajectory pointed toward a successful handover of security responsibilities to Iraqi authorities.

## Political Considerations

The withdrawal timeline unfolds against the backdrop of Iraq's evolving political landscape. Odierno addressed the importance of Iraqi political progress and the formation of a stable government as critical factors in ensuring long-term security gains are not lost.

He stressed that continued diplomatic engagement and support for Iraqi institutions would remain important even as the U.S. military footprint diminishes.

## Looking Ahead

As American forces prepare to draw down, questions persist about the long-term relationship between the United States and Iraq. Odierno indicated that while the combat mission would conclude, ongoing cooperation and partnership could continue in other forms.

The general's remarks reflected cautious optimism about Iraq's future and the ability of its forces to maintain stability after the departure of U.S. troops.

---

*This article is based on General Odierno's appearance on CNN's "State of the Union."*

# U.S. Commander Cites Security Gains in Iraq as Withdrawal Timeline Takes Shape

**BAGHDAD** — The top U.S. military commander in Iraq offered a cautiously optimistic assessment of the country's security situation, pointing to measurable improvements while emphasizing that troop withdrawals would remain tied to conditions on the ground.

Speaking to reporters during a briefing in the capital, the commander noted that violence had declined significantly across several provinces, crediting a combination of coordinated operations, the growing capabilities of Iraqi security forces, and increased cooperation from local communities.

"We are seeing real and sustainable progress in areas that were once among the most volatile," the commander said. "But this progress must be consolidated. Our drawdown will be deliberate and responsible, guided by the situation as it evolves rather than by an arbitrary calendar."

The commander outlined a phased approach to reducing the American military footprint, stressing that the transfer of security responsibilities to Iraqi forces would accelerate as those units demonstrated the ability to operate independently.

## Iraqi Officials Welcome Progress

Iraqi national security adviser Mowaffak al-Rubaie echoed the assessment, framing the improvements as a milestone in the country's push to reclaim full control over its own security.

"The security situation in Iraq has improved beyond our expectations," al-Rubaie said. "We are now in a position where Iraqi forces are taking the lead in protecting our citizens, and this is a source of great pride for our nation."

Al-Rubaie emphasized that the Iraqi government was eager to see a timeline for the departure of foreign troops, while acknowledging the need for continued partnership during the transition.

"We want to see a clear horizon for the withdrawal of coalition forces," he said. "This is not about rushing, but about affirming Iraqi sovereignty. The day is approaching when Iraqis will be fully responsible for Iraq."

He added that ongoing cooperation between Iraqi and American forces remained essential in the near term. "Our partnership has brought us to this point, and we will continue to work closely together until our forces are ready to shoulder the full burden," al-Rubaie said.

## Challenges Remain

Despite the optimistic tone, both officials cautioned that the gains remained fragile. The commander warned that remnants of insurgent groups continued to pose a threat and could attempt to exploit any premature reduction in security presence.

Analysts note that the pace of withdrawal will likely depend on political developments, the effectiveness of Iraqi forces, and the ability of the government to address underlying sectarian tensions.

For now, officials on both sides described the trajectory as encouraging, while stressing that the ultimate goal remained a stable, secure, and sovereign Iraq capable of standing on its own.

---

*This report is a general, illustrative news article. Quotations attributed to named individuals are constructed for the purpose of this example and should not be taken as verbatim statements from actual press events.*

counterfactuals.output:
# Security Conditions Show Signs of Improvement in Iraq, Top Commander Says

**BAGHDAD** — The top U.S. military commander in Iraq offered a cautiously optimistic assessment of the country's security situation, pointing to declining casualty rates and weakened insurgent networks, while cautioning that significant challenges remained.

Gen. Raymond Odierno, commander of U.S. forces in Iraq, told reporters that measurable progress had been achieved across much of the country, though he emphasized that gains remained fragile and reversible.

## Declining Casualties

Odierno noted that troop casualties had fallen substantially compared to the peak violence of previous years. The general attributed the decline to a combination of factors, including the 2007 troop surge, improved cooperation with local security forces, and the growth of Sunni "Awakening" movements that turned against al-Qaeda in Iraq.

"We've seen a significant reduction in attacks against both coalition forces and Iraqi civilians," Odierno said, while cautioning that "any single spectacular attack can still cause considerable casualties and undermine public confidence."

## Insurgent Cells Under Pressure

The general described sustained operations against remaining insurgent cells, particularly those affiliated with al-Qaeda in Iraq, which he said had been degraded but not eliminated.

"These networks have been disrupted, their leadership targeted, and their freedom of movement restricted," Odierno said. "But they retain the capability to carry out periodic high-profile attacks designed to reignite sectarian tensions."

He identified northern cities, particularly Mosul, as remaining areas of concern where insurgent activity persisted.

## Foreign Fighters and Regional Influence

Odierno addressed the continued flow of foreign fighters entering Iraq, singling out infiltration routes through Syria as a persistent problem. He said the number of foreign fighters crossing the border had decreased but remained a threat.

"The majority of foreign fighters continue to enter through Syria," Odierno stated, urging greater cooperation from Damascus in securing the border.

Regarding Iran, the general expressed concern about what he characterized as continued support for Shiite militia groups. He alleged that certain elements provided training, funding, and weapons—including sophisticated roadside bombs—to extremist factions operating inside Iraq.

"We continue to see Iranian influence through their support of Special Groups," Odierno said, referring to breakaway militia elements. He added that this external support complicated efforts to stabilize the security environment.

## Looking Ahead

The commander's remarks came against the backdrop of the U.S.-Iraq security agreement, which set a framework for the drawdown of American forces and the transfer of security responsibilities to Iraqi units.

Odierno stressed that the durability of security gains would ultimately depend on political reconciliation among Iraq's rival factions and the continued development of professional Iraqi security forces capable of operating independently.

"The trends are moving in the right direction," he concluded, "but this remains a critical period, and we must guard against complacency."

---

*Note: This is a composite news-style article reflecting the general themes and positions associated with Gen. Odierno's public statements during this period. Specific quotations are illustrative rather than verbatim.*

# Top U.S. General Expresses Confidence in Iraq Withdrawal Timeline

**Washington (CNN)** — The top U.S. military commander in Iraq voiced strong confidence Sunday that American forces would meet the scheduled deadline for withdrawal, while offering praise for President Barack Obama's role as commander-in-chief.

Speaking on a Sunday morning news program, the general said he was highly confident the drawdown of U.S. troops would proceed on schedule, describing the security situation on the ground as sufficiently stable to support the transition.

"I would rate my confidence very high," the general said when asked to assess the likelihood of meeting the withdrawal timeline. "Iraqi security forces have made significant progress, and we are on track to meet our commitments."

## Assessing the Path Forward

The general acknowledged that challenges remained but emphasized that Iraqi forces had increasingly taken the lead in securing their own country. He noted that periodic violence continued in certain regions but characterized the overall trend as moving in a positive direction.

"There will be difficult days ahead," he cautioned. "But the trajectory is clear, and the Iraqis are stepping up to assume responsibility for their own security."

He added that the responsible drawdown of forces would be conducted in close coordination with Iraqi officials to ensure gains achieved over years of conflict would not be reversed.

## Praise for the Commander-in-Chief

Asked about working with President Obama, the general offered warm assessments of the president's leadership on military matters.

"He has been deeply engaged and asks tough, probing questions," the general said. "He listens to the advice of his commanders on the ground and makes decisions based on sound analysis of the facts."

The general said the president had given military leaders the resources and strategic guidance necessary to accomplish their mission, describing the working relationship as constructive and professional.

## Looking Ahead

The general said that even after the withdrawal of combat forces, the United States would maintain a partnership with Iraq focused on training, advising, and diplomatic engagement.

"Our relationship with Iraq does not end when our troops come home," he said. "It enters a new phase—one built on cooperation and mutual interests."

The comments come as the administration continues to face questions about the long-term stability of Iraq and the broader U.S. strategy in the region.

---

*This is a generic, illustrative article. For reporting on a specific interview, please provide the general's name, the program, and the date so the details can be made accurate.*

# U.S., Iraqi Officials Discuss Security Transition, Troop Drawdown

**BAGHDAD** — Senior U.S. and Iraqi officials met this week to review the transfer of combat responsibilities to Iraqi security forces and to chart the timeline for a reduction in American troop levels, according to statements from both governments.

The talks, held in the Iraqi capital, focused on assessing the readiness of Iraqi army and police units to assume the lead in security operations across several provinces, officials said.

"Our goal remains a sovereign Iraq capable of securing its own territory and its own people," a U.S. official told reporters following the meetings. "The transition will be conditions-based, guided by the capabilities on the ground."

Iraqi officials expressed confidence in their forces' growing capacity while acknowledging that challenges remain in areas such as logistics, intelligence gathering and air support.

"Iraqi forces have demonstrated significant progress," an Iraqi Defense Ministry spokesman said. "We are prepared to take greater ownership of operations, with continued coordination and support from our partners during this period."

## Phased Approach

Under the framework discussed, American forces would shift from a direct combat role toward training, advising and providing specialized support. Officials described the drawdown as occurring in phases, with troop reductions tied to benchmarks measuring the performance of Iraqi units.

Neither side released specific figures on the number of troops to be withdrawn or a firm date for completion, though officials indicated a detailed schedule would be finalized in the coming weeks.

The transition reflects a broader effort to reduce the American military footprint while preserving gains against insurgent and militant groups. Analysts have cautioned that a premature withdrawal could risk security setbacks, while a prolonged presence carries political costs in both countries.

## Regional Considerations

The discussions also touched on regional stability and the need for continued cooperation on counterterrorism, officials said. Both delegations emphasized that the bilateral relationship would endure beyond the drawdown of combat forces.

"This is not an end to our partnership, but an evolution of it," the U.S. official said.

The meetings are expected to continue, with follow-up sessions planned to address the mechanics of the handover and the future of the U.S.-Iraqi security relationship.

*— With reporting from Baghdad.*

---

*Note: This is a template-style wire piece using generic attributions. For publication, specific names, titles, dates and verified quotes should be added.*
